scenario: An order automation starts sending wrong amounts to customers. Three people are already investigating different theories.
question: What should happen first?

options.text: Name an incident lead, contain the damage by pausing the automation, and start a timeline and a status update. Investigate after harm is stopped.
Let each investigator keep digging until one finds the root cause.
Wait for more reports before declaring anything.

why: The first goal is to stop the harm and restore service, even with a workaround. Confusion about who decides is the most common failure.

scenario: You are not sure whether a problem counts as an incident.
question: What does the runbook advise?

options.text: Treat it as one for the first few minutes. It is cheaper to stand down early than to start late, and anyone may raise severity.
Wait until the impact is obvious before telling anyone.
Ask a manager to decide at the next weekly meeting.

why: Severity can be lowered later by the lead. Starting higher costs little compared with a late start.

scenario: A fix does not seem to work. A responder suggests changing three settings at once to save time.
question: What is the better approach?

options.text: Work on the most likely, least risky hypothesis first, make one reversible change at a time and ask the lead before anything that could make things worse.
Change all three, since one of them will probably help.
Roll back everything made so far without recording it.

why: Changing several things at once means you will not know which worked, and you can make things worse. Record every change so it can be undone deliberately.

scenario: A SEV 1 incident is ongoing. Customers and executives are asking for news, but there is no progress yet.
question: What does good communication look like?

options.text: Send updates on the agreed schedule even without progress, say so plainly, use a consistent template and avoid speculating about cause or promising fix times.
Stay silent until there is something positive to report.
Tell customers the vendor is to blame so they stay calm.

why: Silence breeds rumors and duplicate effort. Customers should get honest, specific, calm messages that state what is affected and when the next update comes.

scenario: The incident is resolved. Someone suggests a quick thank-you message and moving on. Another wants to find who made the mistake.
question: What should the review look like?

options.text: A blameless review within a few working days: reconstruct the timeline, explore contributing factors, note what went well and agree on follow-up actions with owners and dates.
Name the individual responsible so it does not happen again.
Skip the review since the incident is closed.

why: People report problems faster when they are not afraid of punishment. Reviews that produce no owned, dated actions teach the team that reviews are theater.
